rio-tinto-valuation-split.headline: Rio Tinto looks fully priced on cash flow, cheap on earnings
rio-tinto-valuation-split.body_md:
Rio Tinto has handed shareholders a 68.5% return over the past five years, and 59.4% over the past twelve months alone. That kind of run usually invites a simple question — is it too late to buy? — and usually gets a simple answer. This time it doesn't.

Run the numbers through a discounted cash flow model and Rio Tinto looks stretched. Using a two-stage free-cash-flow-to-equity approach built on the miner's roughly $6.7 billion in trailing twelve-month free cash flow, the model puts intrinsic value at around £53 a share — against a market price that implies the stock is trading about 26.7% above that mark. On projected cash generation alone, in other words, the market has already priced in more than the discounted flows justify.

Run the same stock through an earnings multiple and the picture flips. Rio Tinto trades at roughly 14.8 times earnings, below the metals and mining industry average of 16.1x and well under the wider peer group's 30.8x. A valuation model tailored to Rio Tinto's growth and risk profile puts a "fair" multiple closer to 21.5x — which would suggest the stock is cheap, not expensive. Tally up the standard valuation checks and Rio Tinto clears just three of six, a split score that reflects a genuinely split picture rather than a rounding error.

## Where the models disagree

The divergence is not noise. DCF models are forward-looking and sensitive to the shape of future cash flows; earnings multiples are backward-looking and sensitive to what the market is currently willing to pay for a dollar of profit elsewhere in the sector. Rio Tinto's problem sits squarely in the gap between the two: the market is paying a below-average multiple for its current earnings, but analysts assessing what those earnings translate into as discounted cash further out are less convinced the growth holds up.

UBS put a name to that concern this year, flagging a "growth gap in the copper pipeline after 2030." Copper output is on track to rise from roughly 883,000 tonnes in 2025 to around 1 million tonnes by 2030, driven by the Oyu Tolgoi ramp-up in Mongolia and Kennecott in Utah. Beyond 2030, the bank sees fewer clear projects ready to fill the gap — Resolution, La Granja and Nuevo Cobre are all longer-dated, and Winu is comparatively small. Rio already holds a 17% stake in Argentina's Los Azules project, a low-cost operation targeting first copper in 2030, and was reported in May to be weighing a larger position there.

![Rio Tinto mine and processing plant](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/63/Rio_Tinto_Boron_mine_and_plant.jpg)

That copper question is precisely what a DCF model is built to capture and a trailing P/E ratio is not. It helps explain why the cash-flow lens flags Rio Tinto as fully priced — it is discounting a growth profile that thins out mid-decade — while the earnings lens, comparing today's profits to today's price, still calls it a discount to peers.

For traders leaning on either signal in isolation, that is the practical takeaway: the multiple says buy, the discounted cash flow says the market has already paid for the easy part. The next real test of which model has it right lands with Rio Tinto's half-year results and any update on Los Azules, where a bigger stake — or a decision to walk away — will tell the market how seriously the company takes UBS's post-2030 gap.

berkshire-abel-playbook.headline: Berkshire's Alphabet and UnitedHealth buys show Abel widening the playbook
berkshire-abel-playbook.body_md:
Greg Abel has been running Berkshire Hathaway for barely six months, and the trades already look different from Warren Buffett's.

Berkshire's first-quarter 13F filing, released May 15, showed Abel exiting 16 full positions — Visa, Mastercard, Amazon, Domino's, Aon and UnitedHealth Group among them — while nearly tripling the company's stake in Alphabet and opening a fresh $2.65 billion position in Delta Air Lines. The portfolio shrank from 42 holdings to 29 in a single quarter. Berkshire was a net seller of stocks for the fourteenth straight quarter, offloading $24.1 billion against $15.9 billion in purchases.

"They're broadening their scope, and they are getting involved," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, in an interview with Benzinga. Woods argues the moves show Abel isn't confined to "the old traditional Warren Buffett investments" and is instead willing to act on positions the market has, in his words, gotten "ridiculously overdone."

## The Alphabet build-out

The clearest evidence for that view is Alphabet. Berkshire held 17.8 million shares worth $5.6 billion at the end of 2025; by March 31 that had grown to nearly 58 million shares, roughly $17 billion — a 224% increase in three months. Then, in June, Berkshire went further, agreeing to buy $10 billion of newly issued Alphabet stock in a private placement tied to the company's $80 billion AI infrastructure raise, split evenly between Class A shares at $351.81 and Class C shares at $348.20. The combined position now stands near $41 billion, about 86.4 million shares and a 9.2% stake — enough to make Alphabet Berkshire's fourth-largest holding, ahead of Coca-Cola. Woods called the scale of it "surprising," noting Berkshire spent 25 years mostly avoiding big technology bets before Apple.

## UnitedHealth complicates the story

The UnitedHealth trade is less a case of Abel expanding the playbook than of him closing a chapter Buffett opened. Berkshire built its roughly 5 million-share, $1.6 billion stake in UnitedHealth in the second quarter of 2025 — under Buffett, after the insurer's stock had collapsed more than 50% — and disclosed it that August. By the Q1 2026 filing, the position was gone entirely. Woods's point stands on its own terms even so: exiting a full stake within a few quarters is "something you didn't see very often from Warren," who tended to hold for years or decades once committed. The speed of the exit, more than the original purchase, is the tell.

That distinction matters for how much weight to put on the "new CEO, new strategy" framing. Buying Alphabet aggressively and funding an AI infrastructure raise is a genuine change in emphasis — Berkshire has rarely written a $10 billion check into unprofitable-by-Buffett's-metrics growth capex. Purging 16 positions in three months, though, reads as much like routine portfolio tidying by a new hand at the wheel as it does a strategic pivot, and Woods himself hedges, saying Abel's full impact "will take time to materialize." He remains bullish on insurance names for the back half of 2026 and expects a buying opportunity in Berkshire shares once the post-Buffett transition fully settles.

The next data point is Berkshire's Q2 13F, due in mid-August, which will show whether the Alphabet buying continues at pace and whether Abel keeps trimming the roster or starts rebuilding it.

hsbc-q2-earnings-outlook.headline: HSBC sees strongest US earnings growth since the pandemic recovery, picks Amazon, Microsoft, Meta
hsbc-q2-earnings-outlook.body_md:
Wall Street's earnings analysts spent much of the past year hedging. Guidance was murky, tariff exposure was unclear, and the AI capital-spending boom looked to some like a bill that would eventually come due. HSBC Global Investment Research is now breaking from that caution in a notably specific way: its analysts expect second-quarter US corporate earnings to grow roughly 22% year-on-year, the fastest pace since the immediate post-pandemic recovery, when reopening comparisons made growth rates look artificially heroic. This time, HSBC argues, the acceleration is real — and it is concentrated in a handful of sectors and companies that happen to include some of the most heavily owned names in the market.

![HSBC's global headquarters at Canada Square in London's Canary Wharf](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/HSBC_Building%2C_Canada_Square%2C_Canary_Wharf%2C_London_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2492384.jpg)

## A revision that moves the wrong way

Earnings estimates typically drift downward as a quarter approaches — analysts trim numbers, companies guide conservatively, and the eventual "beat" is manufactured as much by expectations management as by performance. HSBC's Nicole Inui, head of equity strategy for the Americas, has flagged the opposite happening this cycle: consensus EPS forecasts have been revised *upward* heading into the print, an unusual pattern that HSBC reads as a signal of genuine strength rather than a sandbagged bar.

The growth is not evenly spread. HSBC expects energy and information technology to post double- and triple-digit earnings gains, with semiconductors and tech hardware doing much of the lifting alongside oil and gas producers benefiting from firmer crude prices. Materials names round out the list of standout sectors. Strip those out, and the picture looks far more pedestrian: HSBC puts earnings growth for the rest of the market at around 5%, a reminder that this is a story about a small number of very large, very profitable companies rather than a broad-based recovery.

Inui's own framing is that the acceleration is not the kind of speculative excess that ends badly. "Fundamentally strong sectors and dominant market players," is how she has characterized the source of the growth — a distinction between concentration built on cash flow and concentration built on hope. It is also the same logic behind HSBC's decision in May to lift its year-end S&P 500 target to 7,650 from 7,500, alongside an 8% upgrade to index-level EPS estimates, with strategists sketching a path to 8,000 if AI-driven margins keep expanding and the rest of the market starts to catch up.

## The stock list tech investors already know

HSBC paired the sector call with a list of ten Buy-rated names it considers best positioned for the earnings season now underway: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, AbbVie, Caterpillar, Marriott International, Vertiv, NextPower and Wells Fargo. The rationale, notably, is company-specific rather than a single thematic bet — though the through-line running under most of the picks is the same one driving the sector forecast: artificial intelligence infrastructure spending and the cloud businesses that monetize it.

![Meta's headquarters entrance sign in Menlo Park, California](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/43/Meta_Headquarters_Sign.jpg)

Microsoft's inclusion rests on what HSBC calls a re-acceleration in Azure's AI build-out as infrastructure scales and ecosystem partnerships deepen customer retention. Amazon's case leans on AWS capacity expansion, in-house chip development, and partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI, paired with margin improvement in the retail business. Meta's pitch is narrower and more mechanical: AI-driven ad targeting is lifting monetization per user, while custom silicon and early signs of compute monetization help offset the spending. Both Microsoft and Alphabet have already shown some of this in hard numbers this year — Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 18% to $77.7 billion with Azure growth around 40%, while Alphabet's first-quarter revenue climbed 22% to $109.9 billion.

The rest of the list is a reminder that HSBC's AI thesis extends past the household names. Vertiv, which makes power and cooling systems for data centers, gets a mention specifically because roughly 80% of its revenue is tied to that build-out. Caterpillar's inclusion cites data-center construction demand alongside its traditional mining and infrastructure business. AbbVie, Marriott and Wells Fargo are the outliers — included for company-specific drivers (drug franchise durability, travel demand, net interest income) rather than the AI-capex theme running through the rest of the list.

## Why the margin of safety is getting thinner

![The trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/23/Trading_Floor_at_the_New_York_Stock_Exchange.jpg)

The tension in HSBC's own numbers is worth sitting with. US equities are trading near record valuations, and the case for holding them at those multiples has rested heavily on the assumption that earnings would eventually grow into the price. A 22% EPS print, if it materializes, does exactly that — it closes some of the valuation gap analysts have been uneasy about since late last year. But it does so by leaning further into the same handful of names that already dominate index weightings, which cuts against the standard argument that expensive markets are safer when their gains are broadly distributed.

That is the real stakes of HSBC's call. If energy, tech and materials deliver as forecast while the rest of the market limps along at 5%, the S&P 500's valuation premium becomes even more dependent on a shrinking set of companies continuing to execute flawlessly on AI infrastructure spending that has yet to be tested by a slowdown. A miss from any of Microsoft, Amazon or Meta this earnings season would not just move those individual stocks — it would undercut the sector-level thesis HSBC is using to justify the market's overall valuation.

## What comes next

Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon report second-quarter results within the same two-week window in late July, giving the market a concentrated stress test of HSBC's thesis almost immediately. Energy earnings, tied to crude price moves through the quarter, and early materials reports will offer the first read on whether the acceleration HSBC is forecasting outside mega-cap tech actually shows up, or whether the "broadening" bulls have been waiting for stays confined to the same five or six names.

vodafone-e-stake-sale-spike.headline: Vodafone shares jump 13% as e& exits $6bn stake, lifting FTSE 100
vodafone-e-stake-sale-spike.body_md:
Vodafone Group shares jumped almost 13% in London on Friday, their sharpest single-day move in months, after the UAE telecoms group e& agreed to sell its entire stake in the company for roughly $6 billion. The buyer is not a rival operator or a private equity consortium, but a single French billionaire: Xavier Niel, the founder of Iliad, who now becomes Vodafone's largest shareholder.

The move sits at the odd intersection of an exit and an endorsement. A major investor is walking away with cash in hand, and the stock is rallying anyway — which tells you more about who's buying than who's selling.

## The mechanics of the deal

e& agreed to sell its full 16.21% holding in Vodafone — just under 3.95 billion shares, representing 17.13% of total voting rights — to Vega, an investment vehicle controlled by Niel's family. The agreed price was 112.5 pence per share, a roughly 13-15% premium to Thursday's closing price of 97.76p, putting the total consideration at about £4.4 billion, or $5.95 billion. The package includes cash plus a final dividend of 2.02p per share that Vodafone is due to pay on July 30.

![Vodafone's headquarters campus in Newbury, Berkshire](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/Vodafone_HQ%2C_Newbury.jpg)

For e&, the sale closes out a position it built over four years. The Emirati group bought an initial 9.8% stake in 2022 for about $4.4 billion as part of a stated ambition to become a global telecoms and technology investor, then quietly added to it. On Friday the company framed the exit as "actively managing its investment portfolio while creating value for shareholders" — corporate language for taking a premium and moving on. Analysts read it more bluntly as e& stepping back from that global-platform ambition and banking a gain instead.

## Why a billionaire buying looks like a vote of confidence

The reason the stock didn't just tread water on the news — the reason it jumped — is the identity of the buyer. Niel is not a passive allocator. He built Iliad into France's disruptive fourth mobile carrier in 2012 and now holds telecom assets across nine European countries, including Ireland's eir, with a combined base of roughly 50 million subscribers and more than €10 billion in annual revenue. Buying into Vodafone gives him simultaneous exposure to two of Europe's largest markets, the UK and Germany, where Vodafone has struggled with subscriber losses and a stretched balance sheet.

![Xavier Niel, founder of Iliad](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Xavier_Niel.jpg)

Niel said in a statement that Vodafone was "a compelling investment opportunity, underpinned by quality assets, strong brands, leadership positions and a diversified geographic footprint," and that Vega was "ready to contribute our deep sector expertise and operational know-how." Vega separately said it intends to be "a committed, long-term shareholder," and — pre-empting the obvious next question — stated it does not intend to make an offer for the rest of Vodafone's share capital. Vodafone, for its part, said it would engage with the Niel family group as a supportive, long-term shareholder.

That framing matters for how the market is pricing the deal. A 16% stake changing hands at a premium is one thing; a buyer with an operating track record in the exact markets where Vodafone is under the most pressure is another. Morgan Stanley flagged that the real signal to watch is not the stake itself but how involved Niel's team becomes in Vodafone's operations, particularly in Germany, where the group's cable business has been a persistent drag on earnings.

## A calmer FTSE, for once

The rally in Vodafone was large enough to move the whole London market. The FTSE 100 closed up 24.84 points, or 0.2%, at 10,497.29 on Friday, with Vodafone — up 12.3p to 110.1p — doing most of the lifting alongside a jump in easyJet on a separate takeover approach from Apollo. Traders described the session as calmer than recent ones, a notable shift after weeks in which the index has been jostled by Middle East tensions and rate speculation. A single stock-specific catalyst producing an orderly, well-defined index gain is itself a small tell: when the market can trace a move to one transaction rather than macro noise, it tends to hold.

## What to watch

The transaction still needs regulatory sign-off, expected to conclude by the end of the year, and Vodafone's 2.02p dividend lands on July 30 regardless of how the stake-sale timeline plays out. The more interesting date sits further out: whenever Niel's team starts showing up in Vodafone's German restructuring conversations, or pushes for board representation, the market will get its first real read on whether this was a passive portfolio play or the opening move in something more active. Until then, the 13% jump stands as the market's best guess — that a telecoms operator with a track record of turning around distressed carriers just put $6 billion behind the idea that Vodafone's problems are fixable, not terminal.

ex-elon-etfs-launch.headline: New 'Ex-Elon' ETFs strip Tesla and SpaceX from major indexes
ex-elon-etfs-launch.body_md:
The pitch is almost insultingly simple: buy the market, minus one man.

Subversive Capital, the boutique ETF shop better known for funds that mimic the stock trades of Democratic and Republican members of Congress, has filed with the SEC to launch two new products built around a single exclusion criterion. The Nasdaq-100 Ex-Elon Enterprises ETF (ticker: QQNE) and the S&P 500 Ex-Elon Enterprises ETF (SPNE) will track their namesake benchmarks with one modification — they strip out any company "founded, controlled, or led by Elon Musk," starting with Tesla and the newly public SpaceX.

![Elon Musk](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/34/Elon_Musk_Royal_Society_%28crop2%29.jpg)

## What's actually being excluded

The mechanics are narrower than the headline suggests. QQNE would hold the Nasdaq-100 minus Tesla and SpaceX, which together account for roughly 8.4% of that index's weight. SPNE would hold the S&P 500 minus Tesla alone — SpaceX isn't in the S&P 500 — worth on the order of 2% of that benchmark. Both funds reserve the right to drop future Musk-adjacent companies from their portfolios, naming Neuralink and the Boring Company as candidates should either go public. The filing's own language frames the rationale in risk-management terms: Musk-linked companies, it says, carry "corporate governance concerns, political risks, and heightened share-price volatility" that some investors would rather not underwrite simply by buying an index fund.

That last point is the more interesting one. An investor who buys VOO or QQQ today is, by construction, also buying Musk's governance style, his Twitter/X output, his political ventures and the volatility that comes with a chief executive who runs multiple public companies simultaneously. Subversive's bet is that a slice of the market wants exposure to mega-cap growth without inheriting that particular bundle.

## Why the timing isn't a coincidence

The filing lands three days after SpaceX itself joined the Nasdaq-100, a remarkably fast turnaround for an index that historically required three months to a year of trading history before admitting a new name. Nasdaq changed its own rules in March to allow companies onto the index within 15 trading days of an IPO — a change that arrived just in time for SpaceX's June listing, the largest IPO on record, which raised $85.7 billion and briefly valued the company near $2.1 trillion. Because only a small fraction of SpaceX's shares are currently freely tradeable, its float-adjusted weight in the index started small, but J.P. Morgan estimated the inclusion alone would force roughly $4.3 billion of passive-fund buying as index trackers rebalanced to match.

![SpaceX Falcon 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5d/SpaceX_Falcon_9.jpg)

In other words: millions of index-fund holders who had no opinion on SpaceX, and no ability to opt out, suddenly owned a stake in it the moment the rules changed. That forced, mechanical exposure is precisely what Subversive's new funds are pitched as an escape hatch from.

## Gimmick or genuine risk factor?

Not everyone is convinced this is more than marketing. "They may well attract some money that doesn't think too hard, but these kinds of narrow-cast, micro-ideas aren't really 'for' anyone," said Dave Nadig, president and director of research at ETF.com. "Fun marketing, not a real investment thesis." Morningstar's Jeffrey Ptak was similarly guarded, warning that such a product "might not serve a legitimate investing purpose or cost an arm and a leg for a very marginal benefit," even as he allowed that issuers face pressure to differentiate in an increasingly crowded ETF market. Nate Geraci of NovaDius Wealth Management put a finer point on the fragmentation risk: "if we're now in an ETF world where issuers are excluding single companies from major indexes based on investor sentiment toward one man, we may be slicing things a little too thin."

History offers a caution on both sides. Tuttle Capital's Inverse Cramer Tracker ETF, a similarly personality-driven fund, shut down within a year of its 2023 launch for lack of assets. But Subversive's own congressional-trading funds, NANC and KRUZ, found a durable audience by turning political sentiment into a tradeable product — proof that a narrow thesis can work if the underlying anxiety is real and sustained rather than a passing news cycle.

That's the actual test here. Founder-concentration risk — the idea that an index investor is really making a bet on a handful of individuals rather than diversified corporate management — has been a talking point in equity research for years, applied to Musk, to Mark Zuckerberg's dual-class control of Meta, to Jensen Huang at Nvidia. What's new is that a fund issuer is willing to underwrite that thesis as a product rather than a caveat in a research note, effectively pricing founder dependency as a factor to be hedged rather than merely disclosed.

## What comes next

QQNE and SPNE are slated to begin trading September 21, 2026, structured as actively managed funds under the Tidal Trust I umbrella, competing against index trackers like SPY and QQQ that charge only a few basis points. Whether investors pay up for the exclusion — and whether the funds gather enough assets to survive their first year, the threshold that killed the Inverse Cramer fund — will be the real verdict on whether founder-risk hedging is a durable category or a one-cycle novelty. The nearer-term catalyst to watch is SpaceX's share-lockup expiration, which will free up more stock for trading and could push its Nasdaq-100 weight, and the case for funds like QQNE, higher still.

sk-hynix-nasdaq-debut.headline: SK Hynix's Nasdaq debut marks the largest-ever US listing by a foreign company
sk-hynix-nasdaq-debut.body_md:
SK Hynix closed its first day on the Nasdaq up 13%, at $168.01 a share, capping a listing that raised $26.5 billion and became the largest-ever U.S. market debut by a foreign company. The South Korean chipmaker — the dominant supplier of the high-bandwidth memory that feeds Nvidia's AI accelerators — priced its American depositary shares at $149 apiece, drew orders for more than seven times the shares on offer, and walked away with a listing bigger than Alibaba's $25 billion Nasdaq debut in 2014, the previous record holder.

![The Nasdaq MarketSite tower in Times Square, where SK Hynix rang the opening bell on July 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/81/NASDAQ.JPG)

## A record built on a supply squeeze

The mechanics of the offering matter less than the demand behind it. SK Hynix sold 177.9 million ADRs, each representing one-tenth of a common share, and the deal was covered several times over before pricing. SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won rang the opening bell in Times Square alongside chief executive Kwak Noh-jung, who thanked investors for their "trust and support" and pledged to keep pushing what memory technology can do. Behind the ceremony sits a blunter fact: SK Hynix controls something close to 60% of global revenue in high-bandwidth memory, the stacked-chip technology that sits inside every Nvidia AI accelerator shipped this year, and Kwak has separately warned that 2027 could bring the tightest memory supply the industry has seen. Scarcity, not sentiment, is doing the heavy lifting here — AI-related chip sales at the company have roughly tripled year over year, and HBM now commands three to five times the price of conventional memory.

That scarcity is also why the timing looks deliberate. SK Hynix and Micron both crossed the $1 trillion valuation mark this year as the memory market re-rated around AI demand, and SK Hynix's own market cap moved past $1 trillion within hours of trading. Bringing a U.S. listing to market now, at the peak of investor appetite for anything touching the AI supply chain, is the kind of thing that only works once.

## The discount the debut is meant to close

The more interesting number sits underneath the pop: even after SK Hynix's shares rallied, the company trades at roughly 5.9 times forward earnings against Micron's 7.8 times — despite the two effectively running a duopoly in advanced memory and SK Hynix holding the larger share of the more lucrative HBM segment. Traders and analysts have taken to calling the gap the "Korea discount," a catch-all for the reasons foreign capital has historically underweighted Korean equities: a retail-heavy home market, opaque governance structures at the country's conglomerates, and geopolitical risk tied to Korea's exposure to China and to the broader semiconductor trade fight.

![A high-bandwidth memory die, the stacked chip technology SK Hynix uses to supply Nvidia's AI accelerators](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/AMD%4028nm%40GCN_3th_gen%40Fiji%40Radeon_R9_Nano%40SPMRC_REA0356A-1539_215-0862120_Stack-DSC10301-DSC10363_-_ZS-retouched_%2829514443756%29.jpg/500px-AMD%4028nm%40GCN_3th_gen%40Fiji%40Radeon_R9_Nano%40SPMRC_REA0356A-1539_215-0862120_Stack-DSC10301-DSC10363_-_ZS-retouched_%2829514443756%29.jpg)

That framing is worth treating with some caution — geopolitical risk is real for SK Hynix, which still runs fabs in China, but it is hardly absent for Micron, which sells into the same AI supply chain and carries its own China-market restrictions. A cleaner explanation is simply access: until Friday, U.S. institutional investors who wanted direct, dollar-denominated exposure to the world's leading HBM supplier mostly couldn't get it without navigating the Korea Exchange. The Nasdaq listing removes that friction. Whether it closes the valuation gap will show up over the coming months in whether the ADRs trade in line with the Seoul-listed shares or continue at a discount once the debut-day enthusiasm fades — SK Hynix is due to complete a second listing on the KOSPI on July 29.

## What the appetite signals

Seven-times oversubscription on a $26.5 billion deal is a specific, measurable data point, and it lands at a moment when investors have been hunting for ways to bet on AI infrastructure beyond Nvidia itself. SK Hynix's pitch — first to mass-produce HBM3, first to ship HBM3E, already sampling next-generation HBM4E for Nvidia's Rubin Ultra platform due in 2027 — reads as a "picks and shovels" argument: memory manufacturing requires capital and process expertise that new entrants cannot quickly replicate, which is a different kind of moat than a software company's. That argument evidently found a large and willing audience in New York. It is also being read in Seoul and Taipei as a template. A market with a $26.5 billion appetite for one Korean chipmaker's ADRs is a market other Asian semiconductor firms will now be pricing meetings with their bankers around.

## What to watch

The near-term test is whether SK Hynix's ADRs hold their debut-day gain once trading settles and whether the valuation gap to Micron narrows in the weeks after the KOSPI listing closes the loop on July 29. Micron reports fiscal third-quarter earnings later this summer, which will offer the first direct read on whether the memory pricing cycle Kwak has been warning about — tightening supply into 2027 — is showing up in guidance from the U.S. side of the duopoly as well. If it is, the debate over which company deserves the higher multiple gets a lot more concrete.

nexa-vs-ngloy-value.headline: NEXA or NGLOY: which is the better value stock?
nexa-vs-ngloy-value.body_md:
Zacks' stock-screening desk ran its usual value gauntlet this week on two miners that could hardly look more different up close: Nexa Resources, a mid-cap zinc producer working Peru and Brazil, and Anglo American, the roughly $53 billion London-listed major mid-merger with Canada's Teck Resources. Both trade in New York — Nexa as NEXA on the NYSE, Anglo American as an over-the-counter ADR under NGLOY — and both carry a favourable earnings outlook. On raw valuation, though, they are not close.

Nexa trades around $12.85 a share, a market capitalisation near $1.7 billion, at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 8. Anglo American, at about $24.88 a share and some $52-58 billion in market value depending on the data provider, carries a forward P/E closer to 17.5. Zacks' own scoring system, which sorts stocks into value grades from A to F using multiples like P/E, P/B and cash flow, gives Nexa an A and Anglo American a C. Nexa also holds the stronger Zacks Rank — a #2 (Buy) against Anglo American's #3 (Hold) in the comparison, reflecting sharper upward revisions to analysts' earnings estimates. Put simply: Nexa is cheaper on the numbers and has momentum behind those numbers, which is the combination the Zacks methodology rewards.

![Anglo American's London headquarters at 17 Charterhouse Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b7/17_Charterhouse_Street_1.jpg)

## What's driving each stock

The two companies are betting on different metals cycles. Nexa is a pure zinc play — it runs Peru's largest underground zinc mine at Cerro Lindo and the largest zinc refinery in the Americas at Cajamarquilla — at a moment when the metal itself is not the story; the company's own execution is. First-quarter net income came in at $118 million, up from $29 million a year earlier, with adjusted EBITDA rising 126% to $283 million as zinc production climbed 18% year-over-year on higher ore grades. Net debt sits at $1.48 billion, roughly 2.2 times trailing EBITDA. The company is mid-build on its Cerro Pasco Integration Project, a multi-year expansion meant to extend mine life beyond 15 years, with phase one construction targeted for completion in the third quarter. Zinc itself faces a soft macro backdrop — forecasters at Fastmarkets and StoneX see a growing global surplus into 2026-27 as smelter capacity comes online in China and Europe — which makes Nexa's cheap multiple look less like a bargain and more like the market pricing in that headwind.

Anglo American's story is corporate, not commodity. Shareholders on both sides approved its merger of equals with Teck Resources in December, structured as a share swap — 1.3301 Anglo shares per Teck share — expected to close in late 2026 or early 2027 and to generate roughly $800 million in annual pre-tax synergies. The company also finished divesting its platinum arm, Valterra Platinum, banking $2.5 billion from the final stake sale to pay down debt. That leaves Anglo American a leaner, copper-and-iron-ore-weighted business trading at a premium multiple, with the market effectively paying up for the Teck deal's execution and for copper exposure — a metal that, unlike zinc, is trading near record highs on tight concentrate supply.

The Zacks screen answers the narrow question of which stock is statistically cheaper relative to its own earnings trajectory, and on that measure Nexa wins clearly. Anglo American's higher multiple is the price of admission to a bigger, more diversified, copper-heavy company mid-transformation — a bet on the Teck merger closing cleanly rather than on this quarter's numbers. Whether that premium is justified depends on how the merger integration lands, a question that will start to resolve as the deal moves toward its targeted close.

c3ai-bigbear-ai-comparison.headline: C3.ai and BigBear.ai diverge on revenue, but C3.ai still looks pricey
c3ai-bigbear-ai-comparison.body_md:
Two of the best-known names in publicly traded enterprise AI are moving in opposite directions this year, and the numbers are stark enough to explain why, without any need for hype.

C3.ai, the Redwood City software vendor founded by Thomas Siebel, reported revenue of $51.6 million for the quarter ended April 30 — down 53% from $108.7 million in the same quarter a year earlier. Full fiscal-2026 revenue came in at $250.3 million, while the company's net loss ballooned to $470.4 million, 63% wider than the year before. Siebel, who had stepped back to executive chairman in 2025 after being diagnosed with an autoimmune condition that left him visually impaired, resumed the CEO role on May 8. He arrived to a company that had already cut headcount from 1,075 to 700 as part of a restructuring meant to strip out $135 million in annualized costs.

BigBear.ai, the Virginia-based rival that sells AI and analytics tools mostly to defense and national-security customers, had a far quieter quarter. Revenue came in at $34.4 million for the three months ended March 31 — down just 1% from $34.8 million a year earlier. That follows a rougher 2025, when full-year revenue fell 19% to $127.7 million from $158.2 million, a decline the company has pinned on federal budget cuts under the Trump administration. Backlog, though, grew 14% quarter over quarter to $281.9 million, helped by a $53 million classified contract, and BigBear.ai is sitting on $431.5 million in cash after converting most of its 2029 notes into equity. Management affirmed full-year guidance of $135 million to $165 million.

## The gap between them is closing fast

Put the two most recent quarters side by side and the story sharpens: a year ago, C3.ai was outselling BigBear.ai by roughly $74 million a quarter. Now the gap is about $17 million. That's not BigBear.ai's revenue growing — it's C3.ai's revenue collapsing toward it. Whether that counts as "convergence" is a matter of framing; a more accurate read is that C3.ai's commercial business, hit hard by customer attrition and the disruption around Siebel's medical leave, has fallen off a cliff, while BigBear.ai's government contract book has simply held its ground.

## Priced for a recovery it hasn't delivered

What makes C3.ai worth watching beyond the revenue line is the valuation. The stock trades around $9, having fallen 21% so far in 2026 and 65% from its 52-week high of $35.98 — part of an 82% five-year slide. Yet on a discounted cash-flow basis, Simply Wall St pegs fair value at $6.61 a share, implying the stock still carries a 35% premium. On sales, C3.ai trades at roughly 5.6 times revenue against a peer average closer to 1.6 times. In plain terms: a company burning through cash — free cash flow was negative $199.2 million over the past twelve months — and shedding revenue at double-digit rates is still priced as though a turnaround is already underway. BigBear.ai, at roughly $3.27 a share, doesn't carry the same disconnect, if only because expectations for it were never as lofty.

The next test for both comes with C3.ai's fiscal first-quarter update, expected in September, when investors will see whether Siebel's cost cuts have stemmed the bleeding — and whether the market's optimism about a rebound is catching up with, or still running ahead of, the numbers.

baker-hughes-rig-count.headline: US oil rig count holds flat at 445 as gas rigs edge up
baker-hughes-rig-count.body_md:
The number that usually moves markets didn't move at all. Baker Hughes reported Thursday that the U.S. oil rig count held at 445 for the week, exactly where it sat the week before. Natural gas rigs ticked up by one, to 127. Add in miscellaneous rigs and the total came to 581, against 580 a week earlier — a rounding error dressed up as a data release.

What makes the stall notable is the backdrop. Crude has firmed over the past week, with West Texas Intermediate trading near $71-$72 a barrel — up roughly 3.5% — as renewed U.S.-Iran friction has choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas trade. Higher prices are supposed to be the signal that gets drillers moving. This week, they didn't.

![A horizontal drilling rig used for oil and gas extraction](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d4/Horizontal_Drilling_Rig.jpg)

## Discipline, not direction

The flat print fits a pattern that has held for most of 2026. In the Permian Basin, the country's most active shale patch, the rig count has stayed in the 300-310 range through the first half of the year even as spot prices ran well above what operators had budgeted for. Public producers — the Exxons, Chevrons and Diamondbacks of the sector — have kept capital guidance roughly where it was rather than chase the rally, funneling the extra cash flow into dividends, buybacks and debt paydown instead of new wells. Private operators, who answer to fewer shareholders, have been somewhat more willing to add rigs, but not enough to move the national count.

Part of the reluctance is that the current price strength looks geopolitical rather than structural — a risk premium tied to tanker traffic near Iran, not a shift in the underlying supply-demand balance. Producers who spent the past three years unwinding the growth-at-any-cost habits of the shale boom are in no hurry to reverse course on a headline that could evaporate with a diplomatic de-escalation. At 445 rigs, the oil count remains well below the roughly 498 that Baker Hughes data have averaged since 1987, and a small fraction of the 1,609 peak reached in October 2014.

Gas rigs are a smaller, quieter story. Henry Hub spot prices have drifted between $2.95 and $3.30 per million BTU in recent weeks, pressured by a five-year storage surplus near 185 billion cubic feet and seasonal maintenance at Freeport LNG's export facility. A single added rig is not a vote of confidence so much as noise around a market with ample supply and no urgency to add more.

The next Baker Hughes count lands Friday, July 17, alongside the EIA's weekly petroleum inventory report. Until either the Hormuz risk premium proves durable or storage surpluses start narrowing, the more useful number may not be the rig count itself but how long operators are willing to sit on their hands while it holds.

us-iran-hormuz-pressure.headline: US presses Iran on Hormuz attacks as Tehran vows no surrender
us-iran-hormuz-pressure.body_md:
The Strait of Hormuz has spent the past two weeks doing the opposite of what a 20-billion-barrel-a-year chokepoint is supposed to do: it has emptied out. Tanker traffic through the passage, which normally carries something like a fifth of the world's seaborne oil, was running at roughly 40 transits a day in early July, against a pre-war average of 125 to 140. The gap is the clearest measure of how fragile the truce between the United States and Iran has become, and why crude has been climbing even as neither side wants, on paper, to reopen the war.

![Satellite view of the Strait of Hormuz and the Musandam Peninsula](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Strait_of_Hormuz_and_Musandam_Peninsula_%28MODIS_2018-12-10%29.jpg/1280px-Strait_of_Hormuz_and_Musandam_Peninsula_%28MODIS_2018-12-10%29.jpg)

## A truce that keeps slipping

The current standoff sits on top of a war that formally ended only three weeks ago. US and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28; a ceasefire followed in early April after five weeks of fighting; and on June 17 the presidents of the United States and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum, a mediator-brokered deal giving both sides 60 days to negotiate final terms. Its headline commitments were straightforward — Iran would reaffirm it is not building a nuclear weapon, hostilities would stop on all fronts, and the Strait of Hormuz would reopen to normal traffic.

That 60-day clock is now roughly three weeks from expiring, and the interim has not gone smoothly. On July 6 and 7, Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired on three commercial vessels transiting the strait — a Qatari-owned LNG carrier, the Al Rekayat, which caught fire in its engine room and had to be evacuated, a Saudi-flagged supertanker, and a third ship struck the following morning. It was, by the UN's shipping monitor, the worst single day of attacks since the memorandum was signed, and it prompted fresh US strikes in response. President Trump said afterward he considered the truce effectively over.

## Washington's ultimatum

That episode is the backdrop to the demand US officials confirmed to Reuters on Friday: that Iran issue a public statement declaring every lane of the strait open and its forces no longer firing on ships. "They're either going to give us that statement or we're not having a good outcome for them," one senior official said, describing the choice in blunt terms. Iran's own explanation for the July attacks, relayed to Washington, was that they came from "an errant part of their system" — language US officials read as an admission of an internal split between hardliners still fighting the war on their own terms and a more pragmatic camp trying to hold the memorandum together.

Diplomacy has not stopped despite the exchange of fire. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was expected in Oman on Saturday for talks that Omani mediators hope can stabilize the Hormuz question specifically. Separately, Al Arabiya reported that a four-way call involving the United States, Iran, Pakistan and Qatar was in the works, with US and Iranian technical teams expected to meet in Pakistan on Sunday. Neither report carries confirmed details of what would be discussed, and Gulf mediators — Qatar and Pakistan chief among them, with Turkey, Egypt and Saudi Arabia also making calls — appear to be doing as much improvisation as negotiation, scrambling to keep the memorandum from unraveling rather than advancing it.

![Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/Iranian_Foreign_Minister_Seyyed_Abbas_Araghchi_12th_January_2026.jpg)

## Tehran's line: no surrender

Against that mediation effort, Iran's own negotiating team is not projecting flexibility. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the parliament speaker who has emerged as Iran's chief interlocutor with Washington, said this week that "this conflict will never end with Iran's surrender," and that Tehran is "prepared for an all-out defense" the moment the Americans "betray the understanding." He added that he had told US Vice President JD Vance directly, in negotiations, "we have no trust in you" — and that in his view, only those "prepared for war" are equipped to negotiate with Washington at all.

> "This conflict will never end with Iran's surrender."
> — Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Speaker of Iran's Parliament

![Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Speaker of Iran's Parliament](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Mohammmad_Bagher_Ghalibaf_2025.jpg/250px-Mohammmad_Bagher_Ghalibaf_2025.jpg)

That rhetoric lands as bargaining position more than new escalation — Ghalibaf is restating a line Tehran has held since the ceasefire, not announcing a break from it. But paired with the July 6-7 attacks and Washington's public-statement demand, it illustrates why traders have stopped treating the Islamabad Memorandum as a settled outcome and started pricing it as a conditional one, renewable roughly every time a projectile hits a tanker.

## What the market is actually pricing

Brent crude has held above $76 a barrel, on track for a weekly gain of near 6%, with the premium tied directly to Hormuz uncertainty rather than to demand fundamentals. That is the mechanism worth watching: the strait doesn't need to close to move the price, it only needs traffic to stay thin and the question of who controls it to stay open. Near-standstill shipping volumes are already a supply story even without a formal blockade, and every cycle of attack, strike and demanded statement resets the clock on how much premium the market is willing to hold.

The next concrete markers are close together — Araghchi's Oman meeting and the US-Iran technical session in Pakistan, both expected within days, followed by whatever comes of the mooted four-way call. Behind all of it sits the harder deadline: the Islamabad Memorandum's 60-day negotiating window closes in mid-August, and neither Washington's ultimatum nor Ghalibaf's defiance suggests the two sides are converging faster than that clock is running out.

russia-sanctions-bill-agreement.headline: US senators say they've reached agreement with Trump on Russia sanctions bill
russia-sanctions-bill-agreement.body_md:
Four senators who have spent more than a year trying to force a vote on Russia sanctions say they have finally gotten what they needed most: a nod from the White House. Republicans Lindsey Graham of South Carolina and Roger Wicker of Mississippi, together with Democrats Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, announced on Friday that they had reached agreement with the Trump administration on updated language for the long-stalled Sanctioning Russia Act.

That sounds like a breakthrough, and in Washington terms it is one — the bill has sat in limbo for more than a year despite gathering more than 80 co-sponsors, a veto-proof majority, because Senate Majority Leader John Thune declined to bring it to the floor without assurance the White House wanted it there. What the announcement does not do is specify what changed in the bill's text, or commit Trump to actively pushing for its passage.

![Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of the bill's lead authors, has said the White House has now approved its latest draft.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/Lindsey_Graham_official_photo.jpg)

## The gap the headline skips over

The legislation, as originally drafted, would let Trump impose tariffs of up to 500% on countries that keep buying Russian oil, natural gas or uranium — a list topped by China and India, the two largest importers of Russian crude — with carve-outs possible for nations aiding Ukraine's war effort. That structure has not changed. What has been under negotiation is narrower but consequential: how much discretion the bill hands Trump to waive sanctions or set tariff levels himself, rather than have Congress dictate them.

Shaheen, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's top Democrat, said as recently as this month that "there isn't an agreement on language" on that point, and Democratic caution has hardened since the Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariff authority in March. Friday's statement suggests negotiators found wording both sides can live with, but neither the senators nor the White House released the text, and a spokesperson for the administration did not respond to requests for comment on the record. Graham has told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky the bill has White House backing; Trump himself has not said so publicly since he first endorsed the effort in January.

Thune's position hasn't moved: the Senate will act only once it is certain the administration wants it to, and with midterm-year floor time scarce, that calculus still rests with the White House rather than the 80-plus co-sponsors already on record. A companion House bill cleared the 218-signature threshold this week to force a vote there, which may be the more immediate pressure point.

For markets, the honest read is that nothing has actually shifted yet. Blumenthal himself pointed to the reason the deal became politically easier to strike: oil prices have eased since tensions with Iran cooled, making a tariff threat against Russian crude buyers look less inflationary than it would have looked in the spring. Whether that threat becomes law — and whether Beijing and New Delhi treat it as credible if it does — is the actual catalyst to watch, not this week's framework announcement.

attr-cm-competitive-reshuffle.headline: AstraZeneca's ATTR-CM trial failure reshuffles the field for Alnylam, Pfizer and BridgeBio
attr-cm-competitive-reshuffle.body_md:
A late-stage failure for AstraZeneca and Ionis's Wainua has lifted Alnylam, Pfizer and BridgeBio shares as investors reprice a narrower ATTR cardiomyopathy field, even as AstraZeneca stock slipped.

Rare disease markets often have room for only one or two winners; when a competitor stumbles, the survivor can effectively set pricing and capture the entire addressable patient population. This illustrates how clinical trial outcomes—not fundamentals—drive biotech valuations.

Key facts:
- Which rival company and drug failed, and what specifically happened in their phase III trial (efficacy miss, safety issue, enrollment problem)
- Attruby's current regulatory/clinical status in ATTR-CM and how it compares to the failed competitor
- BBIO stock price at 52-week high: absolute price and % gain over the period

floor.headline: Half the thesis worked
floor.body_md: WMT delivered exactly as the mean-reverter thesis demanded: oversold RSI unwinding cleanly back toward the 20-day moving average, a +27.10 session. But AIV—the highest-conviction pick with RSI at a deep 20.4—went nowhere. Price flatlined at 2.80 in and out. HSY scraped together a modest win. The day's 2-1 record masks the real arithmetic: one trade carried the whole result, the other failed despite everything suggesting it should work. That gap between setup quality and execution is the hinge point. Tomorrow's tape will show whether AIV was just bad timing or a sign that mean reversion's edges have dulled.

floor.headline: Sector Strength, Stock Silence
floor.body_md:
The macro backdrop looked textbook—financials sector running (XLF +1.39% 5d), ABN.AS showing clean relative strength with breakout above both SMAs, HOOD bouncing off a Barclays price target raise. Everything pointed the same direction. The market didn't follow.

HOOD capitulated fastest. Momentum reversed almost immediately after entry, shredding the stop at -3.00% before the news could hold. ABN.AS, the relative strength pick, drifted sideways instead. MUV2.DE exited flat. Three positions, zero follow-through.

The macro thesis wasn't wrong—XLF kept running. The problem was stock-level execution. The sector strength either hadn't reached these names yet, or the individual setups were frontrun. Tomorrow: Was this entry timing, or a signal that macro enthusiasm doesn't guarantee stock-level conviction?

floor.headline: LITE +11% on Meta AI memo; bot never covered photonics despite mega runs
floor.body_md: Lumentum surged 11% on a leaked Meta memo signaling doubled AI-compute spending and custom chip production—pure fiber-optics momentum the bot missed entirely. HPE gained 9.9% on Vultr's AI-datacenter order; SanDisk added 7.6% with no clear catalyst. All three sit outside any active universe: not filtered out by signal rules, but categorically absent from the tradable roster. Lumentum fails classification as optical/photonics despite 700% AI-year runs; HPE looks like legacy enterprise hardware, not the semis/hyperscaler buckets the bot scans. On the downside, AZN.L crashed 7.9% after a heart-drug trial miss—an unscheduled binary event no momentum signal catches. The lesson is structural: today's missed movers aren't signal failures. They're roster gaps that need fixing.
